title: 3 Magnificent Stocks to Buy Before 2027 and Hold for a Decade
detail:
3 Magnificent Stocks to Buy Before 2027 and Hold for a Decade
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) is retaining most of its gains this year despite significant economic volatility and political change. Excitement about artificial intelligence (AI) and confidence in the economy are strong growth drivers, and the market has been rallying after a post-election drop.

But not every stock is enjoying a strong run this year. And while stocks that drop can scare investors, that's where you can often find the best opportunities. Dutch Bros (NYSE:BROS), MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI), and On Holding (NYSE:ONON) are all plunging this year, but they have fantastic long-term potential.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Here's why these three stocks could be great additions to your portfolio.

Image source: Dutch Bros.

1. Dutch Bros: Down 43%

Dutch Bros is a small coffee shop chain with big ambitions. It has created a unique model with exclusive customer beverages and a store portfolio that's mostly drive-thrus, and it has attracted a large customer base that keeps coming back for more.

Part of the company's success comes from its menu, which leans toward the sweet and cold, setting it apart from the classic coffee shop. People also love its friendly customer service and focus on speed.

Management has been at the forefront of beverage innovation, including being the first major chain to offer boba when it became popular two years ago and launching its own line of Myst healthy energy drinks.

Revenue increased 30% year over year in the third quarter, and same-shop sales were up 4.4%. Net income increased from $27.3 million to $37.2 million.

Dutch Bros has 1,273 locations as of the end of the third quarter, and management says it has visibility to reach its goal of 2,029 stores by 2029. That's nearly double today's count, which could lead to doubling revenue over the next four or so years from new stores alone.

The market, however, was disappointed by the lowered full-year guidance. Management is navigating inflation and higher costs, which are impacting the business from top to bottom.

However, the long-term outlook is very strong, and Dutch Bros should reward shareholders who hold for the long term.

2. MercadoLibre: Down 25%

MercadoLibre operates the largest e-commerce business in Latin America as well as a thriving financial platform, including what it expects to become the largest digital bank in Mexico.

Sales consistently grow at a high pace, including a 45% year-over-year increase in the third quarter, driven by a 38% increase in gross merchandise volume and a 53% increase in total payment volume.

The growth is across metrics and businesses. Unique active buyers were up 22% year over year, while items sold per buyer increased 14%. Monthly active fintech users rose 29% over last year, and the credit portfolio was up 62%.

Management is working hard to capture the nascent opportunity as Latin America slowly embraces e-commerce and digital finance. It lags behind other global regions in both areas, yet many of its markets are digitally fluent.

It has many levers to pull to generate higher engagement and growth, including its recently launched Meli+ membership program and a lower free shipping threshold in Brazil. Management is seizing a ripe opportunity to invest for the future, and that's been impacting the bottom line: The operating margin fell from 9.8% last year to 6.3% in the third quarter this year.

The company says that the investments today will lead to a level of scale that will generate even higher profitability, and MercadoLibre stock looks like an excellent buy on the dip.

Image source: On Holding.

3. On Holding: Down 25%

On is a growing athletic wear company that's become popular with affluent shoppers who are more resilient under pressure. The company has been reporting double-digit growth despite inflation, outdoing most of its major competition.

In the third quarter, sales increased 17% year over year, and management reiterated its full-year guidance of low-20s growth. While competitors are struggling to sell in the inflationary environment and forced to mark down inventory, On's gross margin was 72.6% in the quarter, or 66.9% without a tariff refund.

At its recent Investor Day, management said it's significantly ahead of the goals it set for itself at its 2023 Investor Day. It outlined its path to maintain a 65% gross margin through 2029, and in the third-quarter report, it raised the 2026 target to 66%.

On has a growing, resilient business and tons of long-term opportunity, and now is a great time to buy On stock.

Key Takeaways

SCGE Management, a firm that manages $10.4 billion, sold all of its Sea and ServiceTitan shares in the third quarter, its latest 13F shows.

Since Sept. 30, Sea stock has fallen 21% and ServiceTitan stock has risen 17%.

In the same quarter, the fund opened a MercadoLibre position and added 65% to its Snowflake shares.

Sea trades at about 18x forward earnings after growing revenue 43% last quarter, so it looks too cheap to sell, while ServiceTitan's 17% upside at about 56x makes its sale easier to defend.

A firm that manages $10.4 billion just cleared two stocks out of its portfolio.

SCGE Management sold every share it held of Sea (SE:NYSE) and ServiceTitan (TTAN:NASDAQ) in the third quarter, according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13. In the same quarter, it opened a position in MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ), which competes with Sea's Shopee for Brazil's online shoppers, and added to its Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE) stake.

Sea is off the books

At June 30, SCGE held 1.77 million Sea shares worth $170 million, 2.9% of its 13F stocks. By Sept. 30, it held none. Sea stock has fallen 21% since then and sits 49% below its 52-week high. The stock has fallen even though the business is doing well: on Nov. 10, Sea reported third-quarter revenue up 43% to $8.6 billion, and Shopee had its most profitable quarter ever.

ServiceTitan went the other way

SCGE held 1.23 million ServiceTitan shares worth $87 million at June 30, 1.5% of its 13F stocks, and none by Sept. 30. Since then, ServiceTitan stock has gained 17%, though it's still 26% below its 52-week high. Those moves only track the stock price: a 13F shows what a fund held on the last day of each quarter, so it doesn't say what SCGE got for either stock.

title: MercadoLibre vs. Uber Technologies: Which Consumer Network Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

MercadoLibre vs. Uber Technologies: Which Consumer Network Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool

Trading disclosure

Investors searching for high-growth platforms often find themselves choosing between regional dominance and global ubiquity. Whether MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) or Uber Technologies (NYSE:UBER) fits your portfolio better depends on your specific growth objectives.

MercadoLibre serves as the primary digital commerce infrastructure for Latin America, providing essential retail and fintech services. Uber connects millions of consumers with transportation and delivery options worldwide. While both operate platform-based models, they navigate different competitive landscapes and regulatory environments, making this a classic match-up for growth-oriented investors.

The case for MercadoLibre

MercadoLibre operates a vast digital ecosystem that includes its marketplace, the Mercado Pago fintech platform, and a comprehensive logistics network. The company maintains key partnerships with major media brands like Disney+ for its loyalty program and utilizes cloud infrastructure from Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN). It also works with card associations like Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) and Mastercard (NYSE:MA) to facilitate payment services for its millions of active users.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $38.5 billion, which represents a growth rate of approximately 47% over the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $1.9 billion during this same period. This significant growth is a result of expanding electronic commerce adoption and the rising volume of digital payments throughout the region.

The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, is nearly 1.7x. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio of 1.2x indicates its ability to cover short-term liabilities with current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $10.8 billion, providing capital to reinvest in the business among retail stocks.

The case for Uber Technologies

Uber Technologies connects over two hundred million monthly users with mobility and delivery services through its expansive global platform. The company has established significant partnerships with Tractor Supply Company (NASDAQ:TSCO) and Amazon to broaden its reach into grocery and retail delivery. It also relies on third-party mapping and infrastructure software from Alphabet to ensure its services run smoothly across thousands of cities.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, Uber recorded revenue of about $56.5 billion, an increase of roughly 14% compared to the previous twelve-month period. Net income for the company reached approximately $3.5 billion during this time. These results reflect the scale of the platform as it moves toward consistent profitability and stronger bottom-line performance.

Nu Holdings Soars 11% on Record $1.1 Billion Profit as It Takes "First Steps Beyond Latin America" ©@Juan Moyano via Canva, @kanchanachitkhamma via Canva
Key Takeaways

Nu Holdings shares jumped 11% today on record third-quarter net income of $1.1 billion.

Nu is deliberately taking on more credit risk, and its 32% return on equity pays for it.

Nu's loans grew far faster than Itaú Unibanco's and Bradesco's, and it now takes on MercadoLibre in Mexico.

Before today's jump, the stock traded at 4.4x tangible book value, about half its three-year average.

Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE) stock is up 11% today after it reported record third-quarter net income of $1.1 billion, up 31% FX-neutral, after Thursday's close. Founder and CEO David Vélez said the quarter included Nu's "first steps beyond Latin America."

At home, Nu's credit portfolio grew 33% over the year to $41.6 billion, far faster than loans to individuals at Itaú Unibanco (ITUB), up 9.6%, and Banco Bradesco (BBD), up 7.4%. And in Mexico, where Nu just finished its first quarter as a full bank, it goes up against MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ).

TIKR tracks 23 analysts on Nu Holdings. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nu Holdings, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nu Holdings' Analyst Ratings

More profit, and more risk by design

Return on equity hit 32%, but the 90+ day NPL ratio rose to 7.3% from 6.9% in the second quarter.

That's on purpose. "We continue to expand our credit portfolio, deliberately taking some additional risk when the expected returns justify it," CFO Rob Livingston said on the call. Excluding one-off items, Nu's risk-adjusted net interest margin rose to 12.7% from 11.9% in the second quarter.

Itaú's 90-day NPL ratio was 2.0%, barely above 1.9% a year earlier, so the rise in Nu's bad loans looks like Nu's own choice. And Nu's ROE beats Itaú's 23.6%.

Mexico is the next test, where Nu now has 16.6 million customers. MercadoLibre says it gained fintech share there in its own third quarter, but its operating income fell 6% as it reinvested. Can it keep pushing against a full-fledged Nu bank while already giving up margin?

Cheap for a bank growing this fast

Nu also cut its full-year efficiency-ratio forecast to 19%-19.5%, from about 20%.

MercadoLibre Stock Fell 20% in a Month After Hitting a New 52-Week Low. Is the Selling Overdone? ©@small smiles from Getty Images via Canva, @anyaberkut from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre (MELI) stock fell approximately 20% from October 5 to November 10, closing at $1,490.24 after reaching a new 52-week low on November 5.

MercadoLibre's third-quarter revenue and financial income rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but operating margin declined to 6.3% as shipping, fulfillment, and marketing investments pressured profitability.

Sea Limited (SE) reported 41.3% revenue growth at Shopee in the third quarter, while Nu Holdings (NU) provides another perspective on Brazilian consumer credit conditions.

MercadoLibre appears potentially undervalued following the selloff, although stronger margins and continued market share gains will be important to a sustained recovery.

What Happened?

MercadoLibre (MELI) stock declined approximately 20% from its October 5 closing price of $1,860.61 to $1,490.24 on November 10, after hitting a new 52-week low on November 5.

The decline reflects two concerns: political uncertainty in Brazil and weaker-than-expected profitability despite strong revenue growth.

Brazil's October 25 presidential runoff delivered another term for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who defeated Flávio Bolsonaro after trailing him in the first round.

MercadoLibre shares fell approximately 8% on October 26 as investors reassessed Brazil's economic outlook, currency risks, and consumer spending conditions.

Brazil generated approximately $15.2 billion of MercadoLibre's $28.9 billion in 2025 revenue, making it the company's largest market.

However, the company's third-quarter earnings report created a more immediate concern.

According to MercadoLibre's third-quarter financial results, revenue and financial income increased 45% year over year to $10.75 billion, but reported earnings of $8.83 per share fell short of the $9.27 consensus estimate cited in the initial research brief.

Operating margin declined to 6.3% from approximately 9.8% a year earlier, reflecting higher shipping expenses, expanded fulfillment capacity, and increased marketing spending in Brazil.

In its third-quarter shareholder letter, management described the pressure on shipping margins as "the price of the habit we set out to build."

The strategy is producing results. Items sold in Brazil increased more than 40% year over year for the fifth consecutive quarter, while MercadoLibre gained market share across its three largest markets.

Its lower free-shipping threshold also encouraged smaller purchases, initially putting pressure on shipping economics.

By September, Brazilian orders valued between R$19 and R$79 that qualified for free or slower delivery became variable contribution-positive for the first time, suggesting higher order volumes are beginning to improve shipping economics.

Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre stock fell 10% in the week to Nov. 10 after third-quarter EPS came in at $8.83, short of the $9.27 analysts expected, even as revenue rose 45%.

Management chose the squeeze, spending on free shipping and warehouses while Sea Limited's Shopee keeps gaining in Brazil.

Brazil's cost per shipment is falling, and credit held steady, a bar for Nu Holdings ahead of its expected Nov. 12 report.

Analysts still expect an earnings rebound, and the stock trades far below its usual forward multiple.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) stock fell 10% from Nov. 3 to Nov. 10, with most of the damage in a 12% drop on Nov. 5, the day after its report. Revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but EPS of $8.83 missed the $9.27 expected.

That spending comes as Shopee, owned by Sea Limited (SE:NYSE), pushes harder in Brazil, which Sea said on Nov. 10 was again its fastest-growing market. And MercadoLibre's credit sets a bar for Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE), which is expected to report on Nov. 12.

The miss was a choice

Operating income fell 6.6% to $676 million, a 6.3% margin against 9.8% a year earlier. The company paid for more free shipping, added fulfillment space ahead of the holidays and stepped up affiliate marketing in Brazil. CEO Ariel Szarfsztejn told analysts the company is spending because the opportunity in front of it is large. "We have accepted a lower margin to do that," he said.

But the shipping bill is starting to shrink: Brazil's cost per shipment fell 5% from a year earlier in local currency. And in September, orders between R19andR79, which now ship free, paid their own variable costs for the first time.

Shopee is pushing just as hard. It launched four-hour delivery in greater São Paulo in August with more than 4,000 partner stores, and Sea said on Nov. 10 that the service now runs from more than 7,000. MercadoLibre began testing one-hour delivery in parts of the city in September. Sea also said Shopee again grew faster than Brazil's broader market in the third quarter.

Key Takeaways

Danaher and S&P Global are up 23% and 18% since June 30, and MercadoLibre is up 3%.

MercadoLibre has 31% upside to analysts' average target, but its operating margin slipped to 6.3% in the third quarter.

Danaher looks like the best buy of the three, as the only one with a higher average analyst target than a year ago.

Eagle Capital Management, a fund that manages $35.8 billion, made its three biggest adds of the second quarter to MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ), Danaher (DHR:NYSE) and S&P Global (SPGI:NYSE), according to its 13F for the quarter ended June 30, filed Aug. 14.

That filing is still its latest. Since June, two of the three have climbed hard, and over the past year analysts have raised their average target on just one of them.

MercadoLibre is the biggest bet of the three

The fund raised its MercadoLibre stake 79% in the second quarter, to 1.41 million shares worth $2.39 billion at June 30. That's 7.3% of its 13F stocks and its No. 3 position, and the stock is up 3% since.

MercadoLibre reported its third quarter on Nov. 4, and it was more of the same. Revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion. But operating income fell 6% to $676 million, and the operating margin slipped to 6.3%, from 6.7% in the second quarter and 9.8% a year earlier. The company said the drop came from more free shipping, new fulfillment capacity ahead of its peak season and "a tactical decision to increase affiliate marketing spend in Brazil."

The bulls were counting on profit growth, and they didn't get it. Analysts have been lowering their sights all year, too. Their consensus target is down 21% over the past year, to $2,272 from $2,877:

Shares of MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI have plunged 11.9% since the company reported third-quarter 2026 results on Nov. 4, reflecting investor concerns over profitability despite robust revenue growth and continued expansion across its commerce and fintech businesses. The sell-off highlights concerns about the company's aggressive investments in logistics, customer acquisition and financial services, which are supporting engagement but weighing on near-term margins.

Over the past three months, MELI shares have lost 16%, underperforming the industry, the Zacks Retail – Wholesale sector and the S&P 500's decline of 8.7%, 3.1% and 5.7%, respectively. The stock has also lagged Amazon.com, Inc. AMZN, which has dipped 3.6% over the same period. However, MELI has performed better than Sea Limited SE, which has tumbled 31.2%.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

With the stock experiencing significant selling pressure, investors face a key question: Does the recent correction present an attractive entry opportunity, or do persistent margin headwinds warrant caution?

MELI's Q3 Results: What Triggered the Sell-Off?

MercadoLibre reported strong third-quarter 2026 revenue growth, but profitability pressures overshadowed its top-line performance. Net revenues and financial income rose 45% year over year to $10.75 billion, reflecting sustained commerce and fintech momentum. However, income from operations declined 6% to $676 million, while operating margin contracted to 6.3% from 9.8% a year earlier and 6.7% in the preceding quarter.

Net income increased 6% to $448 million, although net margin narrowed to 4.2% from 5.7% year over year. Earnings per share of $8.83 missed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $9.41, adding to investor concerns.

Margin compression primarily reflected higher shipping costs, fulfillment investments and marketing expenses. Net shipping costs created a 60-basis-point sequential margin headwind as lower free-shipping thresholds encouraged smaller, more frequent purchases. Fulfillment capacity expanded nearly 20% sequentially ahead of peak demand, while elevated energy prices increased transportation expenses.

Meanwhile, increased affiliate marketing investments in Brazil pushed sales and marketing expenses up 40 basis points sequentially to 11.6% of revenues. Higher provisions associated with credit portfolio growth also added to year-over-year profitability pressures.

Although these investments aim to strengthen customer engagement and long-term growth, their near-term earnings impact and uncertainty surrounding margin recovery appear to have contributed to the stock's decline.

MercadoLibre (NASDAQ: MELI) is often described as a cross between Amazon.com and PayPal, as it encompasses both a dominant online marketplace (MercadoLibre) and a major "fintech" business (Mercado Pago). You might not have heard of it, though, as it's focused on the Latin American market, which is rather... huge. According to one report, the retail market is valued at $2.0 trillion in 2026 and is expected to reach $3.4 trillion by 2034.

So why is the stock down, and is it worth considering for your portfolio? Let's see.

Meet MercadoLibre

Founded in 1999 and headquartered in Montevideo, Uruguay, MercadoLibre sports a market value near $76 billion (as of Nov. 6). It's active in 18 countries and was recently delivering 3.2 billion items annually. It has 136 million unique buyers and 93 million monthly active users (both numbers as of the third quarter).

That can make plenty of investors skittish, but remember that while the average annual gain over the past three years is just 3.31%, it's 21% over the past 15 years. It can help to be a long-term investor.

Investors worried about MercadoLibre are concerned about factors such as:

Growing competition in the fintech realm.

Potential competition from outside retail giants.

Geopolitical tensions in Latin America, such as in Brazil, where the more business-friendly candidate didn't win the presidential election.

Shrinking profit margins.

Should you invest in MercadoLibre?

Those are quite reasonable concerns, but the company has a lot going for it, as well. And some of those concerns are not as bad as they may seem. For example, the shrinking profit margins are partly due to the company extending more free shipping and credit to shoppers. That can build loyalty and can help it compete against rivals and would-be rivals. It's also due to the company investing in expanding its fulfillment capabilities, which can pay off with better service for customers.

Here are some reasons to be optimistic:

Third-quarter revenue surged 45% year over year.

Engagement is growing among its customers, with items bought per buyer rising 12% year over year, as of the third quarter.

The fintech business is performing well, with monthly active users up 29% and assets under management up 67%. (Mercado Pago is now the largest digital bank in Mexico.)

The Mercado Ads advertising business saw revenue jump 58% year over year in the third quarter.

The ecosystem strategy is working, with the number of customers using both the marketplace and fintech platforms growing by 33%.

Meanwhile, the stock is appealingly priced at recent levels, with a forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 28, well below the five-year average of 50, and a recent price-to-sales ratio of 2.0, well below the five-year average of 4.8.

Long-term investors seeking businesses with solid growth potential, especially those looking for investments based outside the U.S. for diversification, should take a closer look at MercadoLibre.

Why MercadoLibre (MELI) Is Back In The Spotlight

Q3 results put MercadoLibre's earnings mix in focus

MercadoLibre (MELI) just posted fresh third quarter numbers that give you plenty to chew on. Revenue for the period reached US$10.75b, while net income came in at US$448m.

Across the first nine months of 2026, the business reported US$29.76b in sales and US$1.33b in profit. Earnings per share for the quarter were US$8.83 on both a basic and diluted basis.

MercadoLibre's share price has fallen 21% over the past three months and is down 22.34% year to date, even though the 3 year total shareholder return is still positive at 11.2%. This points to fading short term momentum after a stronger earlier run.

Spot opportunities other investors might be missing by scanning our 19 high quality undiscovered gems, featuring fundamentals that are similar to what you are monitoring in MercadoLibre today.

The recent slide in MercadoLibre, despite solid headline revenue and mixed profit trends, puts you at a crossroads. Is this reset already generous enough, or does patience for an even cheaper entry make more sense before running the numbers?

Most Popular Narrative: 36% Undervalued

On the numbers provided, the most followed narrative pegs MercadoLibre's fair value at about $2,395 per share, compared with a last close of $1,532. That gap is what turns the focus onto how much of today's rapid expansion will eventually turn into cash that shareholders actually keep.

According to John_Eric, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the entire debate starts with how you treat MercadoLibre's lending build out and the cash it soaks up.

Under my modeled revenue path, a $1,530 share price can be reproduced if MercadoLibre's owner-cash-flow margin improves from an illustrative starting level near 3.2% to approximately 5.1% over the next decade.

My central case assumes 8.5%.

See why 158 investors see MercadoLibre as 36% undervalued.

Using the narrative's own ten year framework and 11.45% discount rate, the fair value of $2,395 anchors on revenue and financial income progressing from around $40b, while owner cash flow gradually steps up toward that 8.5% margin assumption. The reference price near $1,530 is then essentially the market "pricing in" a milder improvement in cash conversion, closer to the 5.1% margin that backs out of the model when all other inputs stay the same.

That is why the same MercadoLibre financials can support very different conclusions. If operating profitability and owner cash generation trend toward the higher margin path outlined by John_Eric, the narrative argues the current share price undervalues that outcome. If margins stall closer to the lower band, the apparent discount in the headline 36% gap could shrink quickly.
